lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5 you met writing an opinion. What should follow "I think" in an opinion piece? Reasons that explain why.
A claim is what a writer wants you to believe: "Our school should have a garden."
Reasons explain why: "A garden teaches science." Evidence proves it with facts, numbers, examples or experts: "Pupils in a garden project scored higher in science tests."

picture.claim: Our school should have a garden.

lesson.text: A claim is well supported when its reasons are backed by relevant, true evidence. It is weak when it has only opinions, or evidence that doesn't fit.
Watch out: "Everyone knows…" and "It's obvious…" are not evidence.

Try it in the world: make a claim about the best place to build a house in your world. Give two reasons, and one piece of evidence you can check, like "near water: 12 blocks away". Next: the author's point of view.

exercises.prompt: What is a claim?
exercises.hint: The writer's main point.
choices: what a writer wants you to believe
exercises.explain: A claim is what the writer wants you to believe.

exercises.prompt: Which one is evidence?
exercises.hint: Facts or numbers.
choices: Pupils in the project scored 20% higher.
exercises.explain: A measured result is evidence.

exercises.prompt: "Everyone knows it's true" is strong evidence.
exercises.hint: Does it give a fact?
exercises.explain: No: it gives no facts at all.

exercises.prompt: Which one is a reason?
exercises.hint: It explains why.
choices: Our school should have a garden.
exercises.explain: "A garden teaches science" explains why the claim is right.

exercises.prompt: Numbers from a study can be evidence.
exercises.hint: Is a number from a study a feeling or a fact?
exercises.explain: Yes: a study's numbers are evidence.

exercises.prompt: Claim: "Pupils should walk to school." Which evidence supports it best?
exercises.hint: Which one is a relevant fact?
exercises.explain: A health benefit supports walking to school.

exercises.prompt: Which claim has NO evidence?
exercises.hint: Which one only says obviously?
choices: Blue is the best colour, obviously.
Bike lanes cut pollution, a study showed.
Reading daily builds vocabulary, a study found.
exercises.explain: "Obviously" is not evidence.

exercises.prompt: Why is "My cousin thinks so" weak evidence?
exercises.hint: Is it a fact?
exercises.explain: One person's opinion doesn't prove anything.

exercises.prompt: Evidence must fit the claim it supports.
exercises.hint: Would a fact about shoes help an argument about parks?
exercises.explain: Yes: evidence must be relevant.

exercises.prompt: Claim: "The library should open on Sundays." Which reason supports it?
exercises.hint: Why would Sunday help?
choices: Many families are free on Sundays.
exercises.explain: More families could visit.

exercises.prompt: A writer claims chess helps maths and cites a study of 500 pupils. Is this well supported?
exercises.hint: Is a study of 500 pupils evidence?
choices: Yes: a large study is strong evidence.
exercises.explain: A large study is strong, relevant evidence.

exercises.prompt: Which evidence is NOT relevant to "Our town needs a new park"?
exercises.hint: Which one isn't about a park?
choices: Children have nowhere safe to play.
The old park closed last year.
exercises.explain: The mayor's music taste has nothing to do with parks.

exercises.prompt: How could a writer make "Homework should be shorter" stronger?
exercises.hint: What does a claim need, besides being said loudly?
choices: Add facts about sleep and learning.
exercises.explain: Relevant facts make a claim stronger.

exercises.prompt: A claim can have reasons but still be weak if the evidence is false.
exercises.hint: Evidence must be true.
exercises.explain: Yes: false evidence doesn't support anything.

exercises.prompt: Put the parts of an argument in order.
exercises.hint: Start with what you want to prove.
exercises.explain: Claim, reason, evidence, then conclusion.

exercises.prompt: Claim: "Our school should have a garden." Sort each line.
items: A study of 300 schools found this.
exercises.hint: A reason says why; evidence proves it with facts or numbers; "everyone knows" proves nothing.
exercises.explain: Teaching science and building teamwork are reasons. The 20% result and the study of 300 schools are evidence. "Everyone knows" is neither.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of an argument to its job.
exercises.hint: Start with the writer's main point.
exercises.explain: The claim is what the writer wants you to believe; a reason explains why; evidence proves it with facts.

exercises.prompt: Match each claim to the evidence that supports it.
matches: A study: the air got cleaner.
exercises.hint: Evidence must fit its claim: what would prove each one?
exercises.explain: Cleaner air proves the bike-lane claim. Daily readers knowing more words proves the reading claim. Children with nowhere to play shows the town needs a park.

exercises.prompt: Build an argument: put the parts in order.
items: So the library should open on Sundays.
Many families are free on Sundays.
The library should open on Sundays.
A survey: 60 of 80 families would visit.
exercises.hint: Claim first, then why, then the proof, then 'so'.
exercises.explain: Claim: the library should open on Sundays. Reason: many families are free then. Evidence: a survey of 80 families. Conclusion: so it should open on Sundays.

exercises.prompt: Claim: "Our school should have a longer break." Sort each line: strong support, or weak?
items: Our class focused better after play.
A study of 50 schools found the same.
exercises.hint: Strong support can be checked: a fact, a measurement or an expert. 'Obvious' and 'everyone knows' cannot.
exercises.explain: Strong: doctors' advice, what our class noticed, and a study of 50 schools can all be checked. Weak: 'it's obvious' and 'everyone knows' give no facts at all.
